header: IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
General Intelligence and Investigation Inland Revenue and others
PETITIONER BY: Ch. Naeem ul Haq, Advocate
RESPONDENTS BY: Mr. Imran Feroz Malik, Advocate
Mr. Kamran Feroz, I.O/Sr. Auditor, Inland
body: AYYAZ SHAUKAT, J.- Through the instant petition, filed under Article 199 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 (the "Constitution"), the petitioner seeks the quashing of First Information Report (the "FIR") No.02/2025 dated 30.06.2025, registered by the Directorate of Intelligence & Investigation (Inland Revenue), Islamabad (the "Directorate"), under sections 3 and 4 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act, 2010 ("AMLA"), read with section 33(13) of the Sales Tax Act, 1990 (the "Sales Tax Act") and sections 192 and 192A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the "Ordinance"). He also seeks a declaration that the investigation and all proceedings arising from the FIR are without jurisdiction and of no legal effect, inasmuch as no tax liability had been determined against him at the time that the FIR was registered.

2. The facts, briefly stated, are that Syed Muslim Abbas carries on business as a sole proprietor in the name and style of M/s Syed Global Associates. The proprietorship has been registered for sales tax since 21.01.2020. During tax years 2021 to 2024, it supplied food bags and other relief goods, mainly to disaster relief bodies such as PDMA Balochistan, PDMA Punjab, the Red Crescent and Human Appeal. The Directorate found that the sales declared in the income tax returns had not been declared in the sales tax returns. The Directorate summoned the petitioner under section 37 of the Sales Tax Act. In his reply dated 12.02.2025, the petitioner stated that the data was being compiled and that he had applied to the Commissioner under section 74 of the Sales Tax Act for condonation of delay, so that the returns could be revised. The Directorate then forwarded its report to the assessing officer. On 12.06.2025, the Assistant Commissioner W.P No. 4400/2025 2 Inland Revenue issued a show-cause notice under section 11E of the Sales Tax Act, proposing recovery of Rs.250,262,058/-, along with default surcharge and penalties under sections 33(5) and 33(13) of the Sales Tax Act. The hearing was fixed for 26.06.2025.

3. During the pendency of those proceedings, the Directorate registered the impugned FIR on 30.06.2025, upon the complaint of its Deputy Director-II. The FIR alleges that the petitioner collected Rs.211,617,466/- as sales tax from his buyers and failed to deposit it in the national exchequer, which, it is alleged, constitutes tax fraud under section 33(13) of the Sales Tax Act and a predicate offence under Schedule-I of AMLA. It further alleges that he applied the said funds to the acquisition of properties, that his declared business assets rose from Rs.500,000/- in tax year 2023 to Rs.336,028,589/- in tax year 2024, and that his declared income for tax year 2024 was not commensurate with his sales. On this basis, he is also accused of making a false statement in verification and concealment of income under sections 192 and 192A of the Ordinance, with income tax of Rs.113,593,487/- said to be "sought to be evaded". His bank accounts were provisionally attached under section 8(1) of AMLA, with the permission of the learned Special Judge (Customs, Taxation and Anti-Smuggling), Rawalpindi, on 09.07.2025. A notice under section 9(1) of AMLA was issued to him on 15.07.2025. He is stated to be on interim bail. Meanwhile, the adjudication under section 11E of the Sales Tax Act culminated in Order-in-Original No.01/2026 dated 01.10.2025, whereby the petitioner was directed to deposit sales tax of Rs.36,229,363/-, along with default surcharge of Rs.10,144,222/- and penalty of Rs.1,811,468/- under section 33(5) of the Sales Tax Act.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the FIR was registered without any determination of tax liability, when the show-cause notice under section 11E of the Sales Tax Act was still pending. It is urged that, in terms of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Directorate of Intelligence & Investigation-FBR v. Taj International (Pvt.) Ltd. (2025 PTD 1270), no FIR can be registered under the Sales Tax Act unless the tax liability has first been assessed under section 11. He submits that the same principle applies to sections 192 and 192A of the Ordinance, and that no income tax authority has ever returned a finding against the petitioner of false verification or concealment. It is further contended that, in the absence of a predicate offence, there can be no proceeds of crime and, consequently, no offence of money laundering founded upon such proceeds. Learned counsel also points out that seven months had elapsed from the registration of the FIR and yet no report under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 ("Cr.P.C.") had been submitted. He relies on the judgment of this Court in M/s Pakistan Accumulators v. Pakistan through Ministry of Finance (2026 PTD 696) and other judgments discussed hereinafter.

W.P No. 4400/2025 3 5. On the other hand, learned counsel for respondents No.1 to 3 submits that the petition is not maintainable, inasmuch as the petitioner has efficacious alternative remedies under AMLA and the tax laws. It is argued that money laundering proceedings and assessment proceedings operate in separate fields. Under AMLA, the existence of a predicate offence is to be examined on the material available at the time that the proceedings are initiated, and the law does not require assessment to be completed before an FIR is registered. He submits that the FIR was registered after a proper inquiry, which disclosed prima facie sales tax evasion of Rs.211,617,466/- and income tax sought to be evaded of Rs.113,593,487/-, and that the attachment was made strictly in accordance with section 8(1) of AMLA. He further submits that the thresholds in section 33(13) of the Sales Tax Act and sections 192 and 192A of the Ordinance relate to penalty and compounding, and do not bar an investigation. He accordingly prays that the petition be dismissed.
6. I have heard the learned counsel for the parties at length and have perused the record with their assistance.

7. The objection as to maintainability is taken up first. It is correct that this Court does not ordinarily quash an FIR in its constitutional jurisdiction, since the law provides remedies to an accused before the trial court. However, this is not an inflexible rule. Where criminal proceedings suffer from a jurisdictional defect, the High Court is competent to interfere. This Court explained the position in Doctor Nauman Hamid Niaz v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2025 Islamabad 24) as follows:

"[I]t is settled law that criminal proceedings can be quashed or stayed by the High Court, if, in view of the facts of the case, it comes to the conclusion that such proceedings are rooted in malafide or that they suffer from a jurisdictional defect." The petitioner does not invite this Court to appraise the evidence or to adjudicate upon his guilt. His case is that the Directorate had no lawful authority to register the FIR at the stage at which it did. That is a question of jurisdiction. The remedies under AMLA against attachment of property do not furnish an answer to it. This Court, in M/s Pakistan Accumulators v. Pakistan through Ministry of Finance (2026 PTD 696), discussed below, quashed an FIR on this very ground in its constitutional jurisdiction. The objection is, therefore, repelled.

8. The central question that arises for determination is whether an FIR for money laundering, whose predicate offences are offences under the tax laws, can be registered before the tax liability has been determined by the forum provided under those laws. The answer depends, in the first place, on the nature of the offence of money laundering. Under section 3 of AMLA, a person commits the offence of money laundering where W.P No. 4400/2025 4 he deals with property knowing, or having reason to believe, that it is proceeds of crime. Proceeds of crime are defined as property derived or obtained from the commission of a predicate offence, and a predicate offence is an offence specified in Schedule-I of AMLA. The offence of money laundering is thus founded upon a predicate offence. This Court, in Altaf Ahmed Gondal v. Federation of Pakistan (W.P. No.3095 of 2021), while relying on the judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in National Accountability Bureau v. Hudaibya Paper Mills Limited (PLD 2018 SC 296) and Justice Qazi Faez Isa v. President of Pakistan (PLD 2021 SC 1) held:

"In case the proceeds of crime are not relatable to the predicate offences described in the schedule, then offences under the Act of 2010 would not be attracted." In Justice Qazi Faez Isa (supra), the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that the commission of a predicate offence is a necessary element of the offence of money laundering, that proceeds of crime come into being only through the commission of such an offence, and that, in the absence of a predicate offence, an allegation of money laundering cannot be sustained. It was further held that, as the Schedule then stood, mere non-declaration of assets under the Ordinance was not a predicate offence under AMLA.

9. In the present case, the alleged proceeds of crime are not property obtained through any separate or independent criminal act. They are the very sales tax which the petitioner is said to have collected but not deposited, and the very income tax which he is said to have sought to evade. Whether that tax was payable at all, and if so, how much, is precisely the question which the tax laws require the assessing officer to determine. The allegation of money laundering must, therefore, be examined with reference to the statutory requirements governing the particular predicate offences relied upon.

10. As to the predicate offence under the Sales Tax Act, the law is settled by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Directorate of Intelligence & Investigation-FBR v. Taj International (Pvt.) Ltd. (2025 PTD 1270). The Hon’ble Supreme Court, dismissing the appeals of the department and upholding the judgments of the High Courts, held that tax liability is primarily a civil liability, which must be determined through assessment under section 11 of the Sales Tax Act before penal provisions can be invoked. Their lordships observed:

"20...recourse to initiation of criminal proceedings on the allegation of tax fraud, including registration of FIR and arrest of a registered person or any person within the supply chain, amounts to, pre-empting the assessment of tax liability, whereas, in the absence of lawful demand of sales tax pursuant to assessment of tax due, the penal provisions including Section 33 read with sections 37A and 37B cannot be invoked. Therefore, the penal W.P No. 4400/2025 5 provisions including registration of FIR and arrest of any person on the above allegations is without jurisdiction and lawful authority."

"22...[W]e have no hesitation to conclude that without investigative audit or issuance of show cause notice or providing opportunity to explain the matters, registration of F.I.R., initiation of criminal proceeding and arrest of registered person is without jurisdiction and lawful authority. We further hold that criminal prosecution follows adjudication and assessment of tax under Section 11 of the Act, therefore, pre-trial steps including arrest and detention cannot be given effect to unless the tax liability of the taxpayer is determined in accordance with law..."
This judgment is binding on all courts and authorities by virtue of Articles 189 and 190 of the Constitution.

11. The Hon’ble Supreme Court decided Taj International on the law as it stood prior to the Finance Act, 2024, whereby sections 2(37) and 33 of the Sales Tax Act were amended. This Court considered the effect of those amendments in M/s Pakistan Accumulators (supra), which the petitioner has annexed with this petition. It was held that the law laid down in Taj International continues to govern the requirement of prior assessment, and that criminal liability for tax fraud is contingent on the prior determination of civil liability. The Court observed:

"It is thus imperative that the State first determine the civil tax liability of a taxpayer through assessment proceedings undertaken pursuant to Section 11 of the Sales Tax Act. Once such liability is ascertained and quantified on a balance of probabilities, only then can the State then initiate criminal proceedings for purposes of Section 33 of the Sales Tax Act to seek to establish beyond reasonable doubt that the taxpayer is liable for an offence under the said provision and the penalty that follows."

12. Adverting to the facts of the present case, the FIR was registered before completion of the assessment proceedings. The respondents themselves admit in their comments that the contravention report was forwarded to the tax authorities "for assessment of tax liability". The show-cause notice under section 11E was issued on 12.06.2025, and the hearing was fixed for 26.06.2025. Four days after the date fixed for hearing, on 30.06.2025, the Directorate registered the FIR. The figure of Rs.211,617,466/- in the FIR was the Directorate's own projection, which had not been subjected to adjudication. Having itself sent the matter for assessment, the Directorate could not treat the outcome as a foregone conclusion. This is the very course which the Hon’ble Supreme Court has declared to be without jurisdiction and lawful authority.

W.P No. 4400/2025 6 13. Subsequent events demonstrate why the law prescribes this sequence. The adjudication culminated in the Order-in-Original dated 01.10.2025. After allowing for the exempt supplies, the one-fifth portion of sales tax withheld by the buyers, and the input tax available to the petitioner, the Assistant Commissioner determined the principal amount at Rs.36,229,363/-. That is approximately one-sixth of the amount alleged in the FIR. The order imposes a penalty under section 33(5) of the Sales Tax Act, but none under section 33(13), although the show-cause notice had proposed both. I express no opinion on the correctness of this order, which is subject to the remedies provided by the Sales Tax Act. The subsequent assessment thus differs materially from the allegations in the FIR. The reduction in the assessed amount and the absence of a penalty under section 33(13) do not, by themselves, determine criminal liability. The question here remains whether the FIR was lawfully registered before the requisite assessment had been made. The comments of the respondents are silent with regard to this order.

14. As to the predicate offences under the Ordinance, the position is no different. The FIR itself states that sections 192 and 192A of the Ordinance have been treated as predicate offences under Schedule-I of AMLA "as the amount of tax sought to be evaded is more than ten million rupees". The argument of the respondents that this threshold relates only to penalty and compounding is, therefore, misconceived. Under Schedule-I itself, the amount of tax sought to be evaded decides whether these offences are predicate offences at all. That amount can only be determined by the income tax authorities in the manner provided by the Ordinance. Nothing has been placed on record to show that any proceedings were initiated under the Ordinance against the petitioner, or that any income tax authority has found that he made a false statement in verification or concealed his income. The figure of Rs.113,593,487/- appears in the complaint, but the record does not even show how it was computed.

15. This Court dealt with the same question in The State v. Said Jan Afridi (2025 MLD 454), which arose out of AMLA proceedings predicated upon sections 192 and 192A of the Ordinance. The Court laid down the following minimum requirements: "i. The tax authorities under I.T.O shall determine the tax evasion as well as false statement and verification on the basis of tax return or other documents furnished by any person in the proceedings besides the assessment of tax liabilities." "ii. Subject to the prima facie findings of I.T.O, Commissioner Appeals or ATIR with reference to tax evasion and false verification, matter shall further proceeded under AMLA if fulfills the other requirements."

W.P No. 4400/2025 7 The record does not disclose compliance with these requirements in the present case. The petitioner claims that he has since revised his income tax returns. Whether he could do so, and with what effect, is, again, a matter for the income tax authorities, and not for an investigating officer under AMLA.

16. The principal argument of the respondents is that criminal proceedings and assessment proceedings operate in separate fields. Insofar as the initiation of criminal proceedings under the Sales Tax Act is concerned, this contention must be considered in light of Taj International. It is correct that a conviction for the predicate offence is not a condition precedent for a prosecution for money laundering, and that the two may in a proper case proceed together. However, the statutory prerequisites governing the particular predicate offence must still be satisfied. Where the law provides that prosecution for the predicate offence cannot be initiated until the tax liability has been determined, those prerequisites cannot be circumvented merely by invoking AMLA on the same tax allegations. It is a settled maxim that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly (quando aliquid prohibetur ex directo, prohibetur et per obliquum). The powers of attachment and investigation under sections 8 and 9 of AMLA are intended to trace the proceeds of a predicate offence. They cannot be employed to create the predicate offence itself.

17. It follows that the impugned FIR was registered without lawful authority. Once the FIR falls, the proceedings founded upon it cannot survive, sublato fundamento cadit opus (when the foundation is removed, the superstructure falls). These include the investigation, the notice dated 15.07.2025 under section 9(1) of AMLA, and the provisional attachment of the petitioner's bank accounts under section 8(1) of AMLA. The permission of the learned Special Judge for the attachment was likewise sought and granted solely on the basis of this FIR.

18. It must, however, be made clear that nothing in this judgment absolves the petitioner of any tax that is lawfully due from him. The department is free to recover the amount determined in the Order-in-Original dated 01.10.2025, subject to the applicable statutory requirements, any subsisting stay order and the remedies available to either side under the Sales Tax Act. It is equally free to proceed against the petitioner under the Ordinance in accordance with law. If, after the tax liability has been determined by the competent forums, a case of tax fraud, or of false verification or concealment meeting the prescribed threshold, is made out, the competent authorities may proceed under the applicable law, subject to fulfilment of the separate statutory requirements of each enactment. The observations made above are confined to the question of jurisdiction and shall not prejudice the case of either side in any such proceedings. W.P No. 4400/2025 8 19. For the aforementioned reasons, the present petition is allowed. FIR No.02/2025 dated 30.06.2025, registered by the Directorate of Intelligence & Investigation (Inland Revenue), Islamabad, is quashed. All proceedings arising from it, including the notice dated 15.07.2025 under section 9(1) of AMLA and the provisional attachment of the petitioner's bank accounts under section 8(1) of AMLA, are set aside. The respondents shall not take any coercive action against the petitioner on the allegations contained in the FIR, unless his tax liability is first determined in accordance with law. (AYYAZ SHAUKAT)
JUDGE Announced in open Court on 19.10.2026.
